topic.name: Triple Integrals in Spherical Polar Coordinates

question.text: The region $R$ is enclosed inside the sphere $x^2+y^2+z^2=4$ for $x \leq 0.$ Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. \[ \displaystyle \iiint\limits_R (x^2+y^2) \:\textrm{d}V \]
question.explanation:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

\[ \iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \, \mathrm{d}V = \iiint\limits_{\Delta} \, f(\rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \rho\cos\phi) \: \rho^2\sin\phi \: \mathrm{d}\rho \, \mathrm{d}\theta \, \mathrm{d}\phi. \]

If $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

\[ x = \rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \qquad y = \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \qquad z = \rho\cos\phi \]

Notice that the region $R$ represents one-half of the sphere of radius $2$ centered at the origin.

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as

\[ \Delta = \left\{ (\rho, \theta, \phi) \, : \, 0 \leq \rho \leq 2, \: \dfrac{\pi}{2} \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{3\pi}{2}, \: 0 \leq \phi \leq \pi \right\}. \]

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=x^2+y^2{:}$

\begin{align*} f(x,y,z) &= f(\rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \rho\cos\phi) \\[3pt] &= (\rho\cos\theta\sin\phi)^2+(\rho\sin\theta\sin\phi)^2 \\[3pt] &= \rho^2 \cos^2\theta \sin^2\phi + \rho^2 \sin^2\theta \sin^2\phi \\[3pt] &= \rho^2 \sin^2\phi \left( \cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta \right) \\[3pt] &= \rho^2 \sin^2\phi \end{align*}

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

\begin{align*} \iiint\limits_R (x^2+y^2) \: \textrm{d}V & = \iiint\limits_\Delta \rho^2 \sin^2\phi \cdot \rho^2\sin\phi \: \mathrm{d}\rho \, \mathrm{d}\theta \, \mathrm{d}\phi \\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{\pi} \int_{\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\pi/2}}^{\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}3\pi/2}} \int_{0}^{2} \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue} \rho^4 \sin^3\phi} \: \mathrm{d}\rho \, \mathrm{d}\theta \, \mathrm{d}\phi. \end{align*}

example.title: Rewriting a Triple Integral Defined Over a Part-Sphere

question.text: The region $R$ is enclosed inside the sphere $x^2+y^2+z^2=4.$ Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. \[ \displaystyle \iiint\limits_R x\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2} \:\textrm{d}V \]
question.explanation:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

\[ \iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \, \mathrm{d}V = \iiint\limits_{\Delta} \, f(\rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \rho\cos\phi) \: \rho^2\sin\phi \: \mathrm{d}\rho \, \mathrm{d}\theta \, \mathrm{d}\phi. \]

If $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

\[ x = \rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \qquad y = \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \qquad z = \rho\cos\phi \]

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $2$ centered at the origin. As a result, in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as

\[ \Delta = \left\{ (\rho, \theta, \phi) \, : \, 0 \leq \rho \leq 2, \: 0 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi, \: 0 \leq \phi \leq \pi \right\}. \]

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=x\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}{:}$

\begin{align*} f(x,y,z) &= f(\rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \rho\cos\phi) \\[3pt] &= \rho\cos\theta\sin\phi \cdot \rho \\[3pt] &= \rho^2\cos\theta\sin\phi \end{align*}

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

\begin{align*} \iiint\limits_R x\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2} \: \textrm{d}V & = \iiint\limits_\Delta \rho^2\cos\theta\sin\phi \cdot \rho^2 \sin\phi \: \mathrm{d}\rho \, \mathrm{d}\theta \, \mathrm{d}\phi \\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{\pi} \int_{0}^{\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue} 2\pi}} \int_{0}^{\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}2}} \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue} \rho^4 \cos\theta\sin^2\phi} \: \mathrm{d}\rho \, \mathrm{d}\theta \, \mathrm{d}\phi. \end{align*}

example.title: Rewriting a Triple Integral Defined Over a Sphere

question.text: The region $R$ is enclosed inside the sphere $x^2+y^2+z^2=2.$ Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. \[ \displaystyle \iiint\limits_R x^2\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2} \:\textrm{d}V \]
question.explanation:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

\[ \iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \, \mathrm{d}V = \iiint\limits_{\Delta} \, f(\rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \rho\cos\phi) \: \rho^2\sin\phi \: \mathrm{d}\rho \, \mathrm{d}\theta \, \mathrm{d}\phi. \]

If $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

\[ x = \rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \qquad y = \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \qquad z = \rho\cos\phi \]

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $\sqrt 2$ centered at the origin. As a result, in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as

\[ \Delta = \left\{ (\rho, \theta, \phi) \, : \, 0 \leq \rho \leq \sqrt 2, \: 0 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi, \: 0 \leq \phi \leq \pi \right\}. \]

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=x^2\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}{:}$

\begin{align*} f(x,y,z) &= f(\rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \rho\cos\phi) \\[3pt] &= (\rho\cos\theta\sin\phi)^2 \cdot \rho \\[3pt] &= \rho^3\cos^2\theta\sin^2\phi \end{align*}

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

\begin{align*} \iiint\limits_R x^2\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2} \: \textrm{d}V & = \iiint\limits_\Delta \rho^3\cos^2\theta\sin^2\phi \cdot \rho^2 \sin\phi \: \mathrm{d}\rho \, \mathrm{d}\theta \, \mathrm{d}\phi \\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\pi}} \int_{0}^{2\pi} \int_{0}^{\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\sqrt 2}} \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue} \rho^5 \cos^2\theta\sin^3\phi} \: \mathrm{d}\rho \, \mathrm{d}\theta \, \mathrm{d}\phi. \end{align*}

example.title: Rewriting a Triple Integral Defined Over a Sphere

question.text: Evaluate the triple integral \[ \displaystyle \iiint\limits_R 3e^{(x^2 + y^2 + z^2)^{3/2}} \: \textrm{d}V \] over the region $R$ enclosed inside the sphere $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 1.$
question.explanation:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form \[ \iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \, \mathrm{d}V = \iiint\limits_{\Delta} \, f(\rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \rho\cos\phi) \: \rho^2\sin\phi \: \mathrm{d}\rho \, \mathrm{d}\theta \, \mathrm{d}\phi. \]

If $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas: \[ x = \rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \qquad y = \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \qquad z = \rho\cos\phi \]

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $1$ centered at the origin. As a result, in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as \[ \Delta = \left\{ (\rho, \theta, \phi) \, : \, 0 \leq \rho \leq 1, \: 0 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi, \: 0 \leq \phi \leq \pi \right\}. \]

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z) = 3e^{(x^2 + y^2 + z^2)^{3/2}}{:}$ \begin{align*} f(x,y,z) & = f(\rho\cos{\theta}\sin{\phi}, \rho\sin{\theta}\sin{\phi}, \rho\cos{\phi}) \\[5pt] & = 3e^{(\rho^2)^{3/2}}\\[5pt] & = 3e^{\rho^3} \end{align*}

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain
\begin{align*} \iiint\limits_R 3e^{(x^2 + y^2 + z^2)^{3}} \: \textrm{d}V & = \iiint\limits_\Delta 3e^{\rho^3} \cdot \rho^2 \sin{\phi} \: \mathrm{d}\rho \, \mathrm{d}\theta \, \mathrm{d}\phi \\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{\pi} \int_{0}^{2\pi} \int_{0}^{1} 3\rho^2 e^{\rho^3} \sin{\phi} \: \mathrm{d}\rho \: \mathrm{d}\theta \: \mathrm{d}\phi \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{\pi} \sin{\phi} \: \mathrm{d}\phi \cdot \int_{0}^{2\pi} \mathrm{d}\theta \cdot \int_{0}^{1} 3\rho^2 e^{\rho^3} \: \mathrm{d}\rho \\[5pt] &= \big[ -\cos{\phi} \big]_{\phi=0}^{\phi=\pi} \cdot \big[ \theta \big]_{\theta=0}^{\theta=2\pi} \cdot \Big[ e^{\rho^3} \Big]_{\rho=0}^{\rho=1} \: \mathrm{d}\rho \\[5pt] &= -(-1 - 1) \cdot (2\pi - 0) \cdot \left(e^1 - e^0\right) \\[5pt] &= 2 \cdot 2\pi \cdot (e-1)\\[5pt] & = 4\pi(e-1) \end{align*}

example.title: Evaluating a Triple Integral by Converting to Spherical Polar Coordinates

question.text: Evaluate the triple integral \[ \displaystyle \iiint\limits_R \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}} \: \textrm{d}V \] over the region $R$ enclosed inside the sphere $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 16.$
question.explanation:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form \[ \iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \, \mathrm{d}V = \iiint\limits_{\Delta} \, f(\rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \rho\cos\phi) \: \rho^2\sin\phi \: \mathrm{d}\rho \, \mathrm{d}\theta \, \mathrm{d}\phi. \]

If $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas: \[ x = \rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \qquad y = \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \qquad z = \rho\cos\phi \]

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $4$ centered at the origin. As a result, in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as \[ \Delta = \left\{ (\rho, \theta, \phi) \, : \, 0 \leq \rho \leq 4, \: 0 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi, \: 0 \leq \phi \leq \pi \right\}. \]

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}}{:}$ \begin{align*} f(x,y,z) & = f(\rho\cos{\theta}\sin{\phi}, \rho\sin{\theta}\sin{\phi}, \rho\cos{\phi}) \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{\rho} \end{align*}

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain
\begin{align*} \iiint\limits_R \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}} \: \textrm{d}V & = \iiint\limits_\Delta \dfrac{1}{\rho} \cdot \rho^2 \sin{\phi} \: \mathrm{d}\rho \, \mathrm{d}\theta \, \mathrm{d}\phi \\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{\pi} \int_{0}^{2\pi} \int_{0}^{4} \rho \sin{\phi} \: \mathrm{d}\rho \: \mathrm{d}\theta \: \mathrm{d}\phi \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{\pi} \sin{\phi} \: \mathrm{d}\phi \cdot \int_{0}^{2\pi} \mathrm{d}\theta \cdot \int_{0}^{4} \rho \: \mathrm{d}\rho \\[5pt] &= \big[ -\cos{\phi} \big]_{\phi=0}^{\phi=\pi} \cdot \big[ \theta \big]_{\theta=0}^{\theta=2\pi} \cdot \left[ \dfrac{1}{2}\rho^2 \right]_{\rho=0}^{\rho=4} \: \mathrm{d}\rho \\[5pt] &= -(-1 - 1) \cdot (2\pi - 0) \cdot \dfrac{1}{2}(16 - 0) \\[5pt] &= 2 \cdot 2\pi \cdot 8\\[5pt] & = 32\pi \end{align*}
